links.why: When you draw the mango, you look closely and find words for its shape and colour.
Your eyes take in the light bouncing off the thing you are drawing, and your hand copies what you see.
Every drawing is built from circles, squares and triangles put together.

When you mix blue and yellow on the page and get green, you are seeing how colours combine.
The paint spreads in the water because the colour has dissolved and moved with it.
Your painting dries because the water on the paper slowly goes into the air.
More water makes the paint thin and runny, less water makes it thick.
Tell someone which colours you used and what feeling they give.
Clay is soft and bends when wet, which is a property that makes it good for shaping.
When you press and roll the clay, your force changes its shape.

The wheel keeps spinning in a steady way, so the clay stays centred as the potter shapes it.

Folding a square into a triangle shows how shapes can be made from other shapes.

Craftspeople in Rajasthan and Gujarat carve wooden blocks and print cloth by hand.
Natural dyes for blocks come from plants like indigo and from minerals in the ground.

Madhubani painting comes from the Mithila region of Bihar, where women painted walls.

Many natural colours come from plants, like leaves for green and turmeric for yellow.

Madhubani paintings are often made for weddings and festivals.
Gond artists fill animals with dots and lines, so look at how real animals are built.
Gond art comes from the Gond people of Madhya Pradesh.
Small lines and dots fill each shape in a pattern.
Gond paintings often show trees, birds and animals living together.
These paintings tell old stories from the epics, and were shown while the story was sung.
Follow the pictures from one end of the scroll to the other to read the story.
Pattachitra comes from Odisha and Bengal, and kalamkari from Andhra Pradesh.
Many colours come from natural things like stones, leaves and flowers.
Cotton, silk and wool threads are made of very long molecules twisted together.
Cotton thread comes from a plant, silk from a worm, and wool from sheep.
A needle is a wedge, and its sharp point parts the cloth with a small push.
Running stitches and cross stitches make a pattern that repeats.
Thread stays in the cloth because rough fibres grip each other.
Wool is made of very long molecules from sheep, and it can be twisted into yarn.
Knit and purl stitches in a set order make a pattern in the cloth.

People knit in winter to make warm clothes.

Bandhani is a craft of Gujarat and Rajasthan, and leheriya makes waves of colour.
Tying the cloth in the same way gives dots or lines that repeat.
Some natural dyes change colour in sour or soapy water, like red cabbage does.

Folding a card makes a front and a back, and a pop-up uses angles.
Write one clear sentence in your best handwriting.
Raksha Bandhan is a day when sisters tie a rakhi to brothers to show love.
A homemade rakhi shows care because you spent time making it.
Beads and threads in a repeating order make a pattern on the rakhi.
Thread is made of long fibres twisted tight so it is strong.

On Diwali, homes are lit with diyas and lanterns to welcome light.

Clay is soft when wet and hard when dry, so it holds the shape of the idol.
Build it, test it, find what is weak, then make it better.
Measure each piece before cutting so the parts fit together.
Card is light and easy to cut, but a thin straw bends, so choose the material by the job.
A model house stays up when its walls are strong and its base is wide.
Cubes, cylinders and cones are shapes you can build with.
Try a design, see it fall, and build it again stronger.
A tower stays up when it has a wide base and the blocks sit right on each other.
Blocks of different shapes fit together in some ways and not in others.
A block with 2 rows of 4 studs has 2 times 4, which is 8 studs.
If the bridge is too short, think about what to change.

acts.name: Craft from waste (best out of waste)

links.why: A bottle made into a pen stand is reused, so it does not become waste.
Sort paper, plastic and metal first to see which can be used for the craft.
Plastic is waterproof but paper is not, so choose which to use for a plant pot.
Plan what to make, try it, and fix what does not work.
Reusing things means less rubbish for landfills and rivers.
Wet paper and paste dry to a hard shell, which is how the material changes.
The paste hardens as the water in it goes into the air.
Old newspaper is turned into something new instead of being thrown away.
Cover a balloon in layers of paper to make a sphere.
Paper is made from wood, so papier-mache is a plant material.
A camera works a bit like your eye, as light comes through a small hole to make a picture.
The glass lens of a camera bends light to make a sharp picture.
A photo is made of light, so bright places and dark places look different.
Moving closer or farther changes how big things look in the picture.
Tell the story of the picture in a few words.
A shadow forms where an opaque thing blocks the light.
Light travels in straight lines, so the shadow has the same outline as the puppet.
Shadow puppet shows have been done for a long time in Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala.
Tell the story aloud in different voices for each puppet.

Draw the root, stem and leaves to see how each part has a job.
Leaves, flowers and butterflies have matching parts on both sides.
Sketch two leaves side by side and note how they are the same and different.

Look at a fern or a shell: the same shape repeats inside itself.

Green leaves are green because they hold the stuff that makes food from sunlight.
Different plants have leaves of different shapes, edges and veins.
Pressed flowers dry between pages as their water goes out.

Turmeric turns red with soapy water, which is why it can colour a festival.
Beetroot juice colours the water because its colour dissolves in it.
Spinach, beetroot and turmeric are plants that give us both food and colour.
Natural colours wash off safely, but some shop colours have chemicals that harm skin and water.
Sunlight splits into many colours in a rainbow, and paint mixes to make new ones.
The same grey looks darker next to white and lighter next to black.
A coloured thing looks that colour because it sends that colour of light back to your eyes.
Mix in the same amounts each time to get the same colour again.
Mixing half a spoon of yellow with half a spoon of blue shows equal parts.
Your brain can be fooled by lines and shading, so a flat drawing looks deep.
Your eyes see the lines, but your brain decides what they mean.
In a mandala, the same shapes repeat around the middle.
Zentangle fills a space with repeating little patterns.
In a mandala, the same shape repeats around the middle.
Each ring repeats a small design all the way around.
A flower or a snowflake has the same kind of matching parts.
You draw circles with a compass, then divide them into equal parts.
Drawing slowly and calmly can help you feel peaceful.
A kite goes up because moving air pushes against it and lifts it.
The tilted kite pushes the wind down, and the wind pushes the kite up.
The kite is a diamond shape, with two pairs of equal sides.
If the kite spins, change its tail or the strings and fly it again.
A kite needs paper that is light and sticks that are stiff yet bendy.
Wax melts when heated and turns hard when it cools.
Heat makes the wax melt, and when it loses heat it becomes solid again.
Soap lifts dirt and germs off your hands when you wash.
A candle flame needs a wick, wax and air.
Measure the wax or oil carefully to get the same result each time.
Drawing teaches you to look closely at light and shape.
In class you learn which colours go well together.
Drawing an object means breaking it into simple shapes.
Talk about your picture with your teacher and listen to ideas on how to improve it.
Practise a little every day and your hand remembers how to draw.

acts.name: Visiting a museum or art gallery

links.why: Old things in a museum show us how people lived long ago.
Choose one object and describe it so your friend can picture it.
Look at a thing and ask who made it, how, and how we know.
Art in a museum often comes from different parts of India.
Ask the guide a question and listen to the answer.
Look at who built the temple, and how long ago, and what they used.
Many buildings are the same on the left and the right.
Stone, brick and wood each have different properties, and builders choose by need.
People of many religions build places of worship with art on them.
Carved borders, windows and domes show patterns that repeat.
Light falls on one side of an object, so the other side is darker.
A shadow is the dark patch made when an opaque object blocks light.
Making things small and close together far away tricks your eyes into seeing depth.
A drawing of the road shows lines that meet at one point far away.
Draw your home from above, so a friend could find the way.
Use left, right, forward and back to tell where things are.
Mark the shops, the park and the school near your home.
Use a small scale, like 1 cm for 1 metre, to make the map fit.
Plants in pots still need light, water and soil.
The roots stay inside the pot and the leaves grow up into the light.
Waterproof paint helps protect the clay pot from water.
Bright colours look good against green leaves.
Seven shapes can be moved around to make a cat, a house, or a bird.
Try, turn, and try again until the pieces fit.
The small triangle is one half of a bigger one, and a quarter of the square.
Remember which pieces you already tried so you do not repeat.
Pick colours in a set order, like red, blue, red, blue, to make a pattern.
Count the beads you need for one band.
10 beads in each of 4 rows is 4 times 10, which is 40 beads.
Work out how much beads cost to sell the bracelet for more.
Thread is strong because its long fibres are twisted together.
A comic tells a story in a few pictures and a few words.
Read the speech bubbles aloud, in the voice of each character.
A face with eyes, eyebrows and mouth can show happy, sad or angry.

Write the speech bubbles in Hindi or your own language.

A pookalam is round, with rings that repeat around the middle.
Petals, leaves and buds come from different parts of the plant.
Different flowers are available in different seasons.
Group the petals by colour before you lay them out.
Salt is made of tiny crystals with flat faces.

Mixing chalk with salt gives coloured salt that you can pour in layers.
Sort sand, salt and sugar by how they look and feel.
Stamp again and again in a row to make a border.
Your finger feels the paint, which is cold and wet.
A fingerprint has lines that are different for every person.
Count your handprints in a row, then count in tens.

acts.name: Selling your art at a school fair

links.why: Work out the price of each craft and the change to give back.
People buy things they like, and the maker earns for the work.
Many artists and craftspeople earn their living by selling what they make.
Tell a customer about your craft in clear words.
Add up what you earned and take away what you spent.
